hook.text: This orders table is cheap to build and quick to query. It's also wrong: twenty-four rows, and three of the order IDs appear twice.

hook-quiet.text: Nothing errors. Revenue is three hundred thirty-five dollars too high, and every dashboard that reads the table agrees on it.

hook-job.text: An analytics engineer is the last line of defense before a dashboard, so interviews probe how you catch that first: tests, contracts, freshness, and checks on every change.

plan.text: Nineteen questions. Ten are worked through, most on real rows in Postgres, and nine come quickly at the end.

asserts.text: Question one. What does it mean that a dbt test asserts? A test writes an assumption down as a query for the rows that break it.

asserts-zero.text: Zero rows back, and the test passes. Any rows back are the failures, and the run fails with them.

asserts-never.text: It never changes the data. It stops the pipeline loudly, instead of letting bad rows reach a dashboard quietly.

surface.text: Question two. What does a failing uniqueness test actually surface? The rows that break it. A unique test on the order ID compiles to roughly this: group by the key, and keep any key that appears more than once.

surface-run.text: On the page's twenty-four rows, it returns three: orders two, eleven and nineteen, twice each.

surface-fix.text: Those rows are the work. dbt hasn't removed them, and they stay until whatever sent them twice is fixed.

builtins.text: Question three. What are dbt's four built-in generic tests? Here they are in YAML, on an orders model: unique and not null on the order ID, accepted values on the status, and relationships from each customer ID to the customer dimension.
builtins.spoken: Question three. What are dbt's four built-in generic tests? Here they are in yammel, on an orders model: unique and not null on the order ID, accepted values on the status, and relationships from each customer ID to the customer dimension.

builtins-run.text: Each one compiles to a query for its own failures. Here are eight rows, with a problem planted for each test, and every query returns exactly the one it should.

builtins-each.text: Order three, which is there twice. The row with no ID. A status of returned, which isn't on the list. And customer ninety-nine, who isn't in the dimension.

builtins-pair.text: Notice that unique let the missing ID through: a single null isn't a duplicate. That's why unique and not null go together on a key. Together, they say it's a valid primary key.

singular.text: Question four. Generic versus singular tests: what is the difference? Those four are generic: written once, with the column as a parameter, and attached to any column in YAML. Your own generic tests are macros.
singular.spoken: Question four. Generic versus singular tests: what is the difference? Those four are generic: written once, with the column as a parameter, and attached to any column in yammel. Your own generic tests are macros.

singular-sql.text: A singular test is one SQL file for one rule: return every order with a negative amount. Here it returns order seven, at minus twenty-five dollars.
singular-sql.spoken: A singular test is one sequel file for one rule: return every order with a negative amount. Here it returns order seven, at minus twenty-five dollars.

singular-pick.text: So generic for rules you reuse, singular for bespoke business checks. A singular test you find yourself copying into other models wants to become a generic one.

compound.text: Question five. How do you test the uniqueness of a compound key? Order lines have one row per order and line number, so an order ID repeats by design.

compound-wrong.text: A unique test on the order ID alone fails on orders one and three. Order one is fine: it just has three lines.

compound-pair.text: Test the pair, with dbt utils' unique combination of columns, or a singular test that groups by both. It returns only order three's line two, the real duplicate.

compound-grain.text: The test is the grain, written down: one row per order and line number.

fresh.text: Question six. What is source freshness, and how is it different from a test? A test checks what the data says. Freshness checks the clock: how old the newest row is, read from a loaded-at column.

fresh-clock.text: This source warns after six hours and errors after twelve. Its newest row landed at one in the morning. Checked at nine, it's eight hours old: a warning. At two in the afternoon, thirteen: an error.

fresh-valid.text: And all four tests pass on it. The rows that are there are valid; they're just old.

fresh-two.text: So dbt source freshness runs before the models build. It has two thresholds because a feed slipping later each day is the usual signal, and the warning catches the slip before the outage.

ci.text: Question seven. How does CI for analytics typically work? On every pull request, continuous integration runs dbt build on the models that changed, and everything downstream of them.

ci-state.text: It finds the changes by comparing the project with production's manifest, its record of what's deployed. Change the customer staging model here, and three of the four models are built and tested. Orders staging is left alone.

ci-slim.text: That's slim CI: fast feedback without rebuilding every model, and a failing test blocks the merge.

prod.text: Question eight. How do you respond to a failing test in CI versus in production? In CI, the merge is blocked: fix the model or the test before it ships.

prod-sev.text: In production, go by severity. An error halts everything downstream and pages the owner, so the marts keep yesterday's rows instead of taking bad ones. A warning is triaged later.

prod-cause.text: Either way, read the failing rows, decide whether the data or the assumption is wrong, and fix the cause. Never loosen the test just to make it pass.

observe.text: Question nine. What is the difference between testing and data observability? Tests assert rules you wrote in advance.

observe-run.text: Here a day's load drops from thirty orders to twenty. A third of the data is gone, and every test still returns zero rows: the rows that did arrive are fine.

observe-watch.text: Observability watches volume, freshness, schema and distribution against what's normal, and flags the surprise. Tools like Monte Carlo or Elementary add that layer.

observe-both.text: A row-count bound would catch this drop, once someone thinks to write it. Tests catch what you expected; monitoring catches what you didn't.

metric.text: Question ten. How do you test that a metric is correct, not just non-null? Here's a daily revenue model. Not null passes: the number exists. A range test passes too: three hundred fifty dollars is plausible.

metric-recon.text: So reconcile it with an independent source. A singular test compares the day with finance's ledger, within one percent, and returns it: three hundred fifty against a hundred fifty.

metric-why.text: The model joined each order to its items, so an order with three items counted three times.

metric-unit.text: And a unit test would have caught it before it shipped: one mocked order of a hundred dollars, with three items, comes out at three hundred.

r-source.text: Question eleven. What is the difference between a source test and a model test? A source test checks raw data as it lands, and points straight at ingestion. A model test guards your own logic. Do both.

r-where.text: Question twelve. Where should tests live, at staging or in marts? Both. Staging tests catch upstream problems early; mart tests guard the grain and the metrics. Test only at the end, and a bug travels far before it's caught.

r-contract.text: Question thirteen. What is a data contract in dbt? An enforced declaration of a model's column names, types and constraints. If the SQL produces a different shape, the build fails, before any consumer sees it.
r-contract.spoken: Question thirteen. What is a data contract in dbt? An enforced declaration of a model's column names, types and constraints. If the sequel produces a different shape, the build fails, before any consumer sees it.

r-severity.text: Question fourteen. What is test severity, and when do you use warn versus error? Error, the default, fails the run: use it for invariants like a unique key. Warn logs and carries on, for soft signals. Thresholds can warn at one failing row and error at a hundred.

r-fatigue.text: Question fifteen. How do you avoid alert fatigue from noisy tests? Choose those severities deliberately, use the thresholds, and fix or delete tests that fail for known reasons. A suite that cries wolf gets ignored.

r-packages.text: Question sixteen. What extra tests do dbt utils and dbt expectations add? Accepted ranges, expressions that must hold, compound keys, row-count bounds and distribution checks: the sanity checks the four built-ins leave out.

r-unit.text: Question seventeen. What are dbt unit tests, and how do they differ from data tests? A unit test runs a model's logic on mocked rows and compares an expected output, so it runs in CI with no real data. Data tests check the real data in the warehouse.

r-store.text: Question eighteen. What is store failures, and why enable it? It writes the failing rows to a table instead of just counting them, so a red check becomes a dataset you can query.

r-upstream.text: Question nineteen. Why prefer fixing data upstream over patching it in a downstream model? A coalesce in one model hides the defect, has to be copied into every consumer, and anything reading the source still gets bad data. Fix it once, at the source.

next.text: Tests check each model against what you expected of it. They can all pass while two dashboards disagree about revenue. Next: metrics and the semantic layer.
